title: Out of Sight, Out of Mind
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece examines the documented career penalty faced by remote and hybrid workers, who — despite research showing equal or greater productivity — are less likely to be assigned important projects, receive regular feedback, or get promoted compared to in-office peers. The author attributes this gap to the role proximity plays in two organizational essentials: skill development and relationship-building, both of which depend heavily on informal, in-person contact that remote arrangements miss. The piece notes an ironic mismatch, since experienced workers with existing relationships often prefer to work on-site, while less experienced workers who most need visibility prefer remote work.
points: Despite equal or greater productivity, remote and hybrid workers are less likely to be assigned key projects, get regular feedback, or be promoted.
Nearly 90 percent of senior leaders surveyed say they favor in-office workers for assignments, raises, and promotions over remote counterparts.
The career penalty stems from proximity's role in relationship-building and skill development, both of which lean on informal, in-person contact remote work misses.
An ironic mismatch emerges: workers with the least need for in-person visibility (the most experienced) prefer it most, while those who need it most (less experienced) prefer remote work.
quotes: The most recent data overwhelmingly shows fully remote and hybrid workers don’t get assigned the most important projects, fail to receive the same amount of performance feedback, and get overlooked for promotion more often than their in-office counterparts.

In one study, nearly 90 percent of senior leaders and managers suggested that when it comes to favorable assignments, raises, and promotions, they are more likely to reward team members who work every day in the office.
As it turns out, proximity between people is central to two critical aspects of organizational life: skill development, and the building and nurturing of relationships.
Equally important, leaders offer less feedback, check in less frequently, and avoid many of the most important conversations with those they don’t engage face-to-face.
What we do know is this: Relationships sit at the foundation of organizational success.
